channel.title: Cortex
channel.description: A reading list that writes itself, and learns what you know.

item.title: Credibility Theory Is Machine Learning's Shrinkage Estimator
item.description: Bühlmann credibility — the formula that blends a scheme's own claims experience with the industry table — is mathematically identical to the shrinkage estimators behind ridge regression and empirical Bayes, which is exactly why a pricing model without it misprices every small scheme.

item.title: Apple Never Reads Your App Description — Google Play Ranks You on It
item.description: App Store and Play Store search run on almost entirely different inputs, so the keyword strategy that works on one platform can quietly sink you on the other.

item.title: An 80-Year-Old Erdős Conjecture Just Fell to AI — and a Backlog Nobody Can Read Is Piling Up Behind It
item.description: OpenAI's unreleased model produced a proof of an 80-year-old Erdős conjecture strong enough that a Fields medallist says it would pass peer review at the world's top maths journal; most of the hundreds of other AI-generated "solutions" now flooding the field's central problem tracker haven't been checked by anyone qualified to catch a mistake.

item.title: The Best Interests Duty Is a Tie-Break Rule, Not a Vibe Check
item.description: Cert IV teaches best interests duty as an ethical standard. The actual law is a narrow conflict-priority rule that only activates when a broker's pay and a client's outcome genuinely point different ways, and the 2020 commission reforms exist to stop that fight from starting in the first place.

item.title: AI Didn't Remove the Bottleneck in Shipping Software. It Moved It.
item.description: When an agent can write code faster than any person can read it, the limit on how much you can safely automate stops being model quality and starts being how cheaply you can check what came out, and that number is set by your architecture, not your AI.

item.title: The Line-Length Rule WCAG Enforces And Most Apps Ignore
item.description: A type scale fixes size, but two more numbers decide whether anyone finishes reading a paragraph: how many characters sit on a line, and how much space separates it from the next. One of them carries a hard accessibility cap most interfaces blow straight through.

item.title: Your Ankle Can Pass a Hop Test and Still Not Be Ready for Basketball
item.description: Hop tests and a rebuilt training base clear a comeback on slow, controlled loading. Basketball loads the ankle in under a quarter of a second. That gap is real, measurable, and the most common thing a return-to-play checklist misses.

item.title: The Four Questions That Tell You What to Actually Charge
item.description: Anchoring, a value metric, and a four-question survey you can run on your waitlist this week — three concrete moves that replace the guess most solo builders make when they type a number into a pricing page.

item.title: Land Tax Adds Up Your Whole Portfolio — A Trust Gets No Threshold At All
item.description: Land tax isn't assessed property by property — it's the combined site value of everything you hold in a state, and in NSW a discretionary trust loses the $1,075,000 tax-free threshold altogether, turning the vehicle you chose for negative gearing into a much bigger annual bill.

item.title: The Genetic Testing Ban Trades a Capped Risk for an Uncapped One
item.description: The Institute's submission on the government's total genetic-testing ban backs it, rightly — but its own request for population-level monitoring data is the tell that a sum-insured-capped anti-selection risk just became uncapped, with nothing yet priced to replace the cap.

item.title: Oil Just Crashed 8% — the RBA's Inflation Gauge Is Built to Ignore It
item.description: WTI dropped 8.3% and Brent fell below US$90 after a US-Iran ceasefire, but the RBA's trimmed mean measure exists precisely to filter out this kind of shock — so don't expect cheaper petrol to buy the next rate cut.

item.title: Serviceability Runs on Three Numbers Your Client Has Never Seen
item.description: A serviceability assessment doesn't test what a client can afford — it tests a modelled expense floor, a rate buffer nobody pays, and a debt ceiling most borrowers don't know exists. Here's how the three combine, and where each one quietly kills a deal you thought was solid.

item.title: Postgres Will Eventually Refuse Every Write If You Never Vacuum
item.description: Postgres never deletes a row when you tell it to: it marks the old version dead and leaves it on disk, which is why a mass delete doesn't shrink your database and, left unmanaged long enough, why the database can stop accepting writes altogether.

item.title: The Specific Action That Predicts Whether a New User Comes Back
item.description: A signup count and a week-one retention number both hide the same missing metric: the one action, taken in a new user's first session, that separates the ones who become regulars from the ones who quietly vanish, and how to find yours with a spreadsheet and the users you already have.

item.title: Six Fixes Cover 96% Of Why Sites Fail Accessibility
item.description: WebAIM's 2026 scan of a million homepages found 95.9% fail accessibility — but the same six fixable problems, led by low-contrast text, cause 96% of it. What each one actually requires, and when a dropdown is one of them.

item.title: PYS and PMIF Saved Under 1% of a Balance and Broke the Pool
item.description: Run the numbers behind Protecting Your Super and Putting Members' Interests First and the balance protection comes to under 1% of a typical payout, while the opt-in switch adversely selected the shrunken pool of members who kept cover and made everyone who lost it invisible to every experience study since.

item.title: The Comeback Ratio's 0.8–1.3 Sweet Spot Is Partly a Mathematical Illusion
item.description: The acute:chronic workload ratio is the standard tool for pacing a return to sport, but the maths behind its 0.8–1.3 sweet spot also makes it look more predictive than it really is, and that changes how you should use it.

item.title: Westpac's 5% Investor Deposit Is a Hedge, Not a Gift
item.description: Westpac dropped its investor deposit to 5% the same week the Home Guarantee Scheme updated its own rules — one move tightens a subsidy, the other papers over a 34% forecast drop in investor lending, and the LMI bill tells you which is which.

item.title: Why a Rising Signup Count Can Still Mean a Dying App
item.description: A weekly signup count can only go up, but the cohort retention curve — and the "smile" shape at the tail of it — is what actually tells you whether anyone's still opening the app a month on.

item.title: One Postgres Feature Is Why You Don't Need a Database per Customer
item.description: Row-level security enforces tenant isolation inside a single shared database — the mechanism underneath every 'one table, one tenant_id column' app, and the reason schema-per-tenant is a scaling call, not a security requirement.

item.title: One AI Earnings Miss Moved More Than One Stock
item.description: Alphabet's Gemini 3.5 Pro delay helped push the VIX up 6.8% on Thursday even as the ASX 200 climbed — a live lesson in how concentrated an index has to be before one company's news becomes everyone's volatility.

item.title: The Protection Gap Behind Taree's $283 Million Flood Bill
item.description: Taree's flood claims are 92% finalised and the mud is gone — but a $8bn annual insurance tax load and a workers' comp scheme reshuffling its claims managers both point at the same underlying question: who actually carries the risk that goes unpriced.

item.title: Negative Gearing Doesn't Bite Until 1 July 2027 — Fix Your Structure Before Then
item.description: The reform passed a fortnight ago, but the rules that actually change your tax bill don't start until 1 July 2027. That gap is the best window to get title ownership and trust decisions right before the grandfathering window closes.

item.title: The Shift From Task-Driven To Intent-Driven Interfaces
item.description: AI is quietly replacing the desktop metaphor that's run software for forty years. What intent-driven design actually means, why interaction patterns are fragmenting like the 1990s browser wars, and why "faster" AI features often aren't.

item.title: The Shot-Size Ladder That Tells You Where to Point the Camera
item.description: Every frame sits somewhere on a seven-step scale from a tiny figure in a landscape to a single trembling eye. Which rung you pick decides how an audience feels about a moment, before colour, sound or performance ever come into it.

item.title: The Three-Phase Framework for an Ankle Sprain Comeback
item.description: Most rolled ankles get the same blanket advice regardless of how bad the damage actually is. Grading the sprain properly, then progressing by criteria rather than the calendar, is what actually gets you back to cutting and landing safely.

item.title: Benchmarking Your App Against What Actually Converts
item.description: A 2025 benchmark of thousands of live subscription apps found a 400x gap between the top and bottom performers in year-one revenue. The gap isn't the idea — it's three measurable choices you can check against real numbers.

item.title: Putting Numbers on AI's Biggest Costs
item.description: Two studies landed this week trying to quantify what AI actually costs — one on jobs, signed by 200+ economists and 16 Nobel laureates, one on emissions, from a Rice University team measuring how much of a data centre's carbon output could be buried underground.

item.title: The Design System a Solo Builder Actually Needs
item.description: Design systems sound like a big-company problem, but the two dimensions that stop an app looking inconsistent — tokens and governance — fit in one file, even for a team of one.

item.title: Why Speed Is Beating the Rate Sheet in Commercial Lending
item.description: A June 2026 broker survey shows ANZ and Westpac topping usage share in commercial lending — but the numbers that actually decide a deal are turnaround time and credit-assessment satisfaction, not brand habit.

item.title: What Cold Exposure and HRV Actually Do For Recovery
item.description: Two biohacks with real physiology behind them: cold exposure measurably changes your metabolism, and a wearable turns heart rate variability into a daily readiness signal. Here's what the evidence supports and how to use both while you're rebuilding from injury.

item.title: What IAG's RAC Remedy Offer Tells You About Merger Review
item.description: IAG has tabled a competitiveness framework and a repair-facility commitment to get its $1.35 billion RAC Insurance deal past the ACCC. The mechanics of a merger remedy, and why competition regulators care about your combined ratio, in one live case study.

item.title: The Two Numbers That Tell You If Your App Is Actually Working
item.description: A side project can gain users every week and still lose money on each one. Customer acquisition cost and the LTV:CAC ratio are the two numbers that tell the difference — and why the manual, unscalable acquisition phase is what makes them trustworthy.

item.title: Volatility Just Cratered — Here's What Markets Are Betting On
item.description: The VIX fell to a 2026 low of 15.03 overnight while the S&P 500 and ASX 200 both pushed higher. Read together with a firmer AUD and softer gold, it's a textbook risk-on signal — and it says something specific about how markets are pricing the AI capex build-out.

item.title: Broking's Next Growth Line Isn't Home Loans Anymore
item.description: Three Broker Daily stories published the same day describe one shift: SME clients are borrowing to survive rather than grow, aggregators are racing into commercial and SMSF lending to catch them, and none of it works on top of a dirty CRM.

item.title: What AI Is Actually Doing Inside Australian Life Insurers
item.description: The Actuaries Institute's Life Insurance Data and AI Working Group named six live AI use cases in Australian life insurers — and none of them makes a pricing or reserving call. A second Institute session the same fortnight explains why that gap matters.

item.title: Every Shot You Take Comes Down To Three Dials Fighting Each Other
item.description: Aperture, shutter speed and ISO trade off against each other in every frame you shoot, and video adds a fourth rule photography doesn't need. Here's how the three dials work, and why pushing ISO to fix a dark shot makes it look worse, not better.

item.title: Why Some Screens Feel Instantly Organised And Others Feel Like A Wall Of Buttons
item.description: Two Nielsen Norman Group breakdowns of Gestalt grouping explain why some interfaces read as organised at a glance: proximity and similarity are doing the work before anyone reads a word, whether or not you designed for them.

item.title: AI Isn't Discovering New Science Yet — It's Automating the Grunt Work Behind It
item.description: A new Argonne National Laboratory framework runs chemistry experiments from plain English, and a University of Tokyo team upgraded nanoparticle analysis with pure software. Neither discovers anything new — and that's exactly why the pattern matters.

item.title: Why Some Indie Apps Rank for Thousands of Searches and Yours Doesn't
item.description: Programmatic SEO built Wise's 4.67 million monthly organic visits from one template. The difference between that and a Google spam penalty comes down to two things most indie builders skip: real data, and matching the page to what the searcher wants.

item.title: The New-Build Tax Edge Is Real — So Is the Sales Pitch Riding On It
item.description: A buyer's agency is marketing new builds hard off last week's negative gearing news, with a July 2027 date attached. The underlying tax edge checks out — the pitch built on top of it needs a harder look.

item.title: The Numbers That Actually Clear You to Play Again
item.description: 'Ease back in' isn't a return-to-play criterion. Sports medicine has a harder one: the limb symmetry index and a battery of hop tests — and even a passing score has a catch worth knowing.

item.title: AI Can Draw The Screen Now — Your Job Is Judging Which One's Right
item.description: Two design essays published this week converge on the same shift: once AI generates the screen and the code behind it, the designer's real work becomes judgment and explanation, not production.

item.title: General Insurance's FY26 Squeeze: Underwriting Tightens, Distribution Consolidates
item.description: Suncorp's FY26 trading update shows a $250m natural hazard miss and falling investment income squeezing underwriting margin, while Austbrokers Countrywide's post-merger leadership reshuffle shows distribution consolidating around the same pressure.

item.title: Two Lenders Just Changed Leaders — Most Brokers Won't Notice In Time
item.description: ANZ picked up a new board director from NAB's business bank and Bank of Sydney made its acting CEO permanent — plus the time-blocking habit that decides whether you're the broker who actually benefits from it.

item.title: Every Channel Decays — The Manual Work That Buys You Time First
item.description: Every acquisition channel decays from the day you find it. The founders who last are the ones who do the unscalable, manual work first, and use it to build the taste that picks the next channel well.

item.title: How Embeddings Make 'Relevant' a Computable Thing
item.description: Retrieval-augmented generation depends on one mechanism to decide what counts as relevant: turning meaning into vectors you can measure the distance between. Here's how that works, and where it lives in a Next.js/Supabase stack.

item.title: Aperture, ISO, and the Shutter Speed Rule Unique to Video
item.description: The three controls that expose every shot — and the one rule, specific to video, that photography tutorials rarely mention.

item.title: The US Jobs Miss That's Quietly Repricing Australian Mortgage Rates
item.description: US payrolls badly missed forecasts overnight and Fed rate-hike odds collapsed — a shift that reaches Australian bank funding costs before the RBA does anything at all.

item.title: The Third Interstellar Comet Turns Out to Be 12 Billion Years Old
item.description: New James Webb spectroscopy on 3I/Atlas, only the third confirmed interstellar visitor, shows chemistry that doesn't match anything born in our solar system, and puts its age at up to 12 billion years.
